# #57407 [ROCm][Perf] Enable layer-aware CSA2 multi-stream overlap for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash

https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/57407 · shen-shanshan · MERGED · created 2026-09-17T15:42:14Z · merged 2026-09-27T15:48:02Z

## Purpose

DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash has three attention layer shapes: full CSA2 layers (2/8/14/20) run SWA + compressor + indexer and build a new global KV cache with their own Top-K indices; reindex CSA2 layers (24/28/32/36) run SWA + indexer only, re-scoring Top-K over an earlier layer's global KV cache; all other layers are dense or pure SWA.

The shared v4.1 pipeline overlaps the full CSA2 layers with **three** fork/join pairs per step (input projections; Q/SWA-insert vs compressor; indexer vs cache-insert) and the reindex layers with one. On ROCm each fork/join is a HIP event pair per side stream, so the multi-stream launch cost outweighs the overlap benefit there.

---

This PR gives the ROCm attention layer a layer-type-aware scheme with exactly one fork/join per step:

**Full CSA2 layers (`_forward_csa2_full`)**: one 3-stream fork right after the input norm.

- default stream: fused wqa+wkv → q/kv split+norm → wq_b → fused qnorm/RoPE/SWA-insert;
- aux stream 0: the compressor chain (kv_score GEMM → save/compress/norm → RoPE-quant cache insert);
- aux stream 1: indexer `weights_proj`.

After the single join, the indexer K write (`_produce_k`, whose `wk` consumes the aux-0 latent) and the query path (`forward_q`, whose wq_b consumes the default-stream qr) run serially, followed by the indexer op and sparse MLA. **Reindex CSA2 layers (`_forward_csa2_reindex`)**: the input projections run serially first (the query path consumes qr, so overlapping the weight projection is not worth it), then one 2-stream fork overlaps the SWA q path with the indexer query path. **Dense layers**: fully serial (`aux_stream_list` disabled). --- A new shared helper `execute_in_parallel_default_first` (in `vllm/utils/multi_stream_utils.py`) mirrors `execute_in_parallel` but enqueues the default chain before the aux chains — the default chain is the longest, so starting it first shortens the step tail while the aux streams still only wait on the pre-fork default-stream work. The fork is gated exactly like the shipped v4.0 multi-stream gate (#51794/#56853): it only runs where the fork/join becomes static graph edges (inside capture, or with non-dict metadata such as the profile run); everywhere else — including MRV1, which keeps its wide eager region (#51430) — the layer falls back to the fully sequential base pipeline. The CUDA/NVIDIA path is untouched except for a behavior-neutral base refactor: the v4.1 indexer's query path is extracted into `DeepseekV4Indexer.forward_q`, still driven unchanged by the base `forward` (`_produce_k` keeps its private name). This is not a duplicate of #51794/#56853, which cover v4.0: v4.1-flash has a different topology (the indexer derives K from the kv-source compressor's latent, with no indexer-local compressor), so the overlap must differ per layer type. ## Trace Comparison (Take conc=4 as an example) **With regard to CSA2 layers with compressor and indexer (layer_id=2/8/14/20):** Before:

> The default NV path launches multi-stream 3 times per layer, which is inefficient on ROCm path (multi-stream cost > overlap benefit). After (**20.76%** faster than the old pattern): --- **With regard to CSA2 layers only with indexer (layer_id=24/28/32/36):** Before: > No need to overlap indexer weight projection, since the benefit (4 μs) < the multi-stream cost (5 μs + 6 μs = 11 μs). Instead, we prefer to overlap SWA process and indexer process. After (**11.90%** faster than the old pattern): ## Test Plan Benchmark with SA InferenceX `8k1k` workload with server launch commands below: ```bash export VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER=1 VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER_MOE=1 export AITER_TRITON_LOG_LEVEL=ERROR VLLM_USE_BREAKABLE_CUDAGRAPH=1 export OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 VLLM_ENGINE_READY_TIMEOUT_S=3600 export VLLM_USE_RUST_FRONTEND=1 PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 GPU_COUNT=4 export HF_HOME=/shared/models vllm serve deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash \ --host 0.0.0.0 \ --port 8333 \ --tensor-parallel-size 4 \ --language-model-only \ --tokenizer-mode deepseek_v41 \ --tool-call-parser deepseek_v41 \ --enable-auto-tool-choice \ --reasoning-parser deepseek_v41 \ --moe-backend aiter \ --gpu-memory-utilization 0.9 \ --max-model-len 1048576 \ --max-num-seqs 128 \ --max-cudagraph-capture-size 1024 \ --max-num-batched-tokens 16384 \ --disable-uvicorn-access-log \ --no-swa-bounded-replay \ --engram-config '{"cpu_offload":false}' \ 2>&1 | tee "${OUTDIR}/server.log" ``` Accuracy test with `gsm8k` dataset using `lm_eval`:

```bash
lm_eval \
  --model local-completions \
  --model_args model=deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash,base_url=http://0.0.0.0:8333/v1/completions,num_concurrent=64,max_retries=10,max_gen_toks=2048,timeout=60000,tokenized_requests=False \
  --batch_size auto \
  --tasks gsm8k \
  --num_fewshot 5 \
  --output_path . 2>&1 | tee -a eval.log
```

> [!NOTE]
> All tests based on latest `nightly-rocm100` image.

## Test Result

### Benchmark

By the way, note that the e2e benefit could be small, since there are onlt **8** layers that we can optimize (overlap), while other layers always execute serially.

| Conc | Version | Output token throughput (tok/s) | Change  | Mean TTFT (ms) |  Change  | Mean TPOT (ms) | Change  |
| ---: | :------ | ------------------------------: | :-----: | -------------: | :------: | -------------: | :-----: |
|    1 | main    |                          114.47 |    —    |         392.61 |    —     |           8.32 |    —    |
|    1 | this PR |                          117.28 | 2.45% ↑ |         266.06 | 32.23% ↓ |           8.25 | 0.84% ↓ |
|    4 | main    |                          381.72 |    —    |         348.33 |    —     |           9.86 |    —    |
|    4 | this PR |                          386.47 | 1.24% ↑ |         331.76 | 4.76% ↓  |           9.76 | 1.01% ↓ |
|   16 | main    |                         1018.13 |    —    |         496.96 |    —     |          14.73 |    —    |
|   16 | this PR |                         1018.69 | 0.06% ↑ |         495.02 | 0.39% ↓  |          14.73 |  0.00%  |
|   64 | main    |                         1912.44 |    —    |        1165.33 |    —     |          31.71 |    —    |
|   64 | this PR |                         1920.10 | 0.40% ↑ |        1160.00 | 0.46% ↓  |          31.59 | 0.38% ↓ |

In summary, the performance data indicates that this PR provides consistent throughput gains and latency reductions without introducing a regression in the tested metrics. The most noticeable benefit is at low concurrency, while at higher concurrency (conc=16 and 64) the changes are comparatively small, suggesting that the optimization has limited additional impact once the system becomes heavily loaded.
